reasons: No tests or validation for the data are visible in the code shown.
Several industries are marked STUB, and the meaning of that status is not written in the file.
The strategic sector appears in the sector list, but no industry using it is visible in the parts shown.

terms.meaning: the agreed family tree of categories used to label each project
the specific category a project is filed under, such as a particular type of reactor
a short fixed identifier for an industry, such as nuclear, used in code to find it
a broad group that contains several industries, such as energy
an industry status that the file uses for industries not yet fully ready, with the exact meaning not written here

sections.name: File setup, IndustryStatus, IndustryStructureType
sections.title: Imports and allowed status labels
sections.what: Brings in brand constants and defines the only two allowed status labels (live or stub) and the two allowed structure styles (value chain or sub-industries).
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Fixed labels help keep the status and structure fields consistent across the app.
sections.watch_out: Changing these labels requires updating every place that reads them.

sections.name: IndustryNode
sections.title: Shape of a taxonomy node
sections.what: Defines what one node in an industry tree holds: a name, an optional description, and optional child nodes. Children can nest further, so trees can be several levels deep.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The nested structure lets one shape describe segments, categories and leaves.

sections.name: Industry
sections.title: Shape of an industry record
sections.what: Defines the fields every industry must have, such as slug, name, sector, status, structure type, tree, and key metrics. Some fields such as project count and taxonomy notes are optional.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It gives every industry the same layout so other code can rely on it.
sections.watch_out: Adding a required field here means every industry entry must be updated to include it.

sections.name: SECTORS
sections.title: List of sector groupings
sections.what: Lists the six sectors that group industries, each with an id, a display name and a short tagline. The app uses these ids to group industries on screens.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Grouping keeps the home page organized by broad area.
sections.watch_out: The sector id on each industry must match one of these ids exactly.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_FIRMS
sections.title: Consulting firm names and shared note
sections.what: Lists the consulting firms whose segmentations the taxonomy is said to draw on, adds the brand firm list, and builds one sentence that names them all.
sections.why: The note tells users where the taxonomy comes from, so the source is written once and reused for each industry.
sections.watch_out: These firm names are claims about where the taxonomy comes from. Confirm them before publishing the note.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 1)
sections.title: Nuclear power industry, first part
sections.what: Defines the nuclear power industry: its name, description, sector, status, and a tree starting with uranium mining, conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication, and reactor construction.
sections.why: Nuclear is the only industry with a strict classification rule, so its tree defines which values are accepted.
sections.watch_out: Renaming any node here changes which nuclear records are accepted during ingestion.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 2)
sections.title: Nuclear rest, then oil and gas start
sections.what: Finishes the nuclear tree with reactor types, operations and life extension, and spent fuel and decommissioning. Then it defines the oil and gas industry with its six segments, such as offshore field development and refining.
sections.why: Each industry is listed in full in this part of the file, so the tree stays with its owner.
sections.watch_out: The file is split by line count, not by industry, so one industry can span two sections.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 3)
sections.title: LNG and gas infrastructure industry
sections.what: Defines the liquefied natural gas industry with four value-chain stages: liquefaction, shipping, regasification, and storage and distribution.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It is written in the same layout as the other value-chain industries.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 4)
sections.title: Renewables industry, first half
sections.what: Defines the renewables and storage industry and starts its tree with solar, onshore wind, offshore wind, hydropower, and geothermal.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each renewable technology is a separate branch so that projects can be filed under one.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 5)
sections.title: Renewables end, power grid start
sections.what: Finishes the renewables tree with closed-loop geothermal and battery storage. Then defines the power transmission and grid industry with HVDC links, AC transmission, and substations.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 6)
sections.title: Power grid end, hydrogen start
sections.what: Finishes the grid tree with smart grid and distribution. Then defines the hydrogen economy industry, which starts with production pathways, storage and transport, and end uses.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The hydrogen industry is marked STUB, so its tree may be incomplete.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 7)
sections.title: Hydrogen end, mining and battery metals
sections.what: Closes the hydrogen industry and defines the mining and metals industry. Its first branch covers battery metals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and some rare earths.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The mining industry has three levels of nesting, so a value may sit one or two levels below its parent.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 8)
sections.title: Rare earths, graphite and base metals
sections.what: Continues the mining tree with rare earths, graphite, and other critical minerals. It also starts the base metals branch with copper, aluminum and zinc.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 9)
sections.title: Zinc, lead, precious metals and steel start
sections.what: Finishes zinc and covers lead, then the precious metals branch with gold, silver and platinum group metals. It starts the iron and steel branch.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 10)
sections.title: Steel end, coal, lithium, gas power
sections.what: Finishes iron and steel, then defines coal. It also defines the lithium mining industry and the gas-fired power industry, which says records with no asset class get no sub-industry.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Lithium appears both inside the mining tree and as its own industry.
sections.watch_out: Lithium is listed in two places with similar but not identical trees, so edits in one may not appear in the other.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 11)
sections.title: Chemicals industry, first part
sections.what: Defines the chemicals and petrochemicals industry and starts its tree with olefins and polymers, aromatics and polyester, fertilizers and nitrogen, and specialty chemicals.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The chemicals industry is marked STUB.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 12)
sections.title: Chemicals end, dairy start
sections.what: Finishes chemicals with industrial gases. Then starts the dairy industry, with its header, the taxonomy note, and the first plant types: fluid milk, cheese, and butter and ghee.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Dairy is the only food industry in the file.
sections.watch_out: The dairy taxonomy note is cut off in the text provided, so its full wording cannot be checked.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 13)
sections.title: Dairy plant types, middle
sections.what: Lists the dairy plant types for yogurt, milk powder, whey and protein concentrates, casein, ice cream, and the start of infant formula.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each dairy plant type is a separate branch so projects can be filed under one.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 14)
sections.title: Dairy plant types, later
sections.what: Finishes infant formula and lists condensed milk, cream and desserts, plant-based alternatives, upstream farms, cold chain, and by-products.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Upstream and downstream items are included so a project can be recorded from farm to shelf.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 15)
sections.title: Dairy end, rail transit start
sections.what: Closes the dairy industry with its key metrics and starts the rail and transit industry, defining its header and high-speed rail branch.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 16)
sections.title: Rail stations end, ports start
sections.what: Finishes the rail industry with metro, light rail, freight, and stations and depots. Then defines the ports and maritime industry with container terminals and bulk terminals.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 17)
sections.title: Ports end, water industry
sections.what: Finishes ports with shipyards and waterways. Then defines the water and wastewater industry with desalination, wastewater treatment, dams, and bulk water transfer.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 18)
sections.title: Real estate, first part
sections.what: Defines the real estate industry and starts its tree with residential, retail, office, and hospitality.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 19)
sections.title: Real estate end, data centers start
sections.what: Finishes real estate with industrial and logistics and mixed-use developments. Then defines the data center industry with hyperscale campuses and colocation.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 20)
sections.title: Data center rest, semiconductor start
sections.what: Finishes the data center tree with edge sites, subsea cables, and terrestrial fiber. Then starts the semiconductor fabs industry with its wafer fabrication branch.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The semiconductor and data center industries are both marked STUB, so their trees may be incomplete.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 21)
sections.title: Semiconductor tail and battery supply chain start
sections.what: Finishes the semiconductor industry entry with its equipment and wafer plant suppliers, then starts the battery entry with its material and refining groups. Each group holds named plant types with short descriptions that the app can show as a tree.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The file is one long list so that each industry can be edited on its own.
sections.watch_out: The battery entry is filed under the sector 'digital' while its status is STUB, which may be a mistake, so check it before relying on sector grouping.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 22)
sections.title: Battery chain end and defense industry start
sections.what: Finishes the battery entry with its pack assembly and recycling groups, then starts the aerospace and defense entry with its shipbuilding and aircraft groups. Every group follows the same shape of name, description and plant types.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The repeated shape lets the app show every industry the same way.
sections.watch_out: The aerospace and defense entry is marked STUB, so the app may present it as incomplete, and its status must be kept in step with its content.

sections.name: INDUSTRIES (part 23)
sections.title: Defense munitions and space infrastructure groups
sections.what: Lists the missile, munitions and space groups for the aerospace and defense entry, then closes the main list of industries. The app's industry list comes from this list.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Each entry must be followed by a comma and the list must be closed properly, because one missing bracket breaks the whole file.

sections.name: getIndustry
sections.title: Find one industry by its web name
sections.what: Returns the industry whose slug matches the given text, or nothing if no industry matches. The slug is the short web-friendly name used in addresses.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets other parts of the app open one industry from its address without searching the list themselves.
sections.watch_out: The caller must handle the nothing result, because a mistyped slug gives no error, only empty output.

sections.name: getIndustriesBySector
sections.title: List industries in one sector
sections.what: Returns every industry whose sector field matches the given sector id. Likely used to group industries on sector pages.
sections.why: Likely reason: sector pages need a filtered list without repeating the search logic.
sections.watch_out: Sector ids are compared exactly, so a changed or misspelled sector id silently removes industries from its group.

sections.name: countAllNodes
sections.title: Count every node in a tree
sections.what: Counts all items in a nested tree of plant groups and sub-items, including items inside items. An empty or missing tree counts as zero.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives a size figure for an industry's structure. The code does not show where the figure is displayed.
sections.watch_out: This counts parent groups as well as final plant types, so it is not the same as the number of plant types a user can pick.

sections.name: countLeafNodes
sections.title: Count final plant types only
sections.what: Counts only the items at the bottom of the tree, the ones with no sub-items. A group with an empty sub-list is also counted as a final item.
sections.why: Likely reason: final items are the plant types a user can choose, so this count is the more useful number to show.
sections.watch_out: A group whose sub-list is empty is counted as a final item, which can inflate the number.

sections.name: SourceType
sections.title: Allowed kinds of source publisher
sections.what: Lists the seven allowed categories of a source, such as industry association, government, vendor or academic. These are the only labels a source can carry.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps source types consistent so they can be filtered or labelled the same way.
sections.watch_out: Adding a new kind here may also require changes in any code that displays or filters sources by type.

sections.name: TaxonomySource
sections.title: Shape of one publisher record
sections.what: Describes what each publisher entry must contain: an id, a short name, a full name, a kind, a rank from 1 to 3, an optional country and a description. Citations point to these publishers.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the field names. The rank is probably used to show how authoritative a source is, but the code here does not show that.
sections.watch_out: The rank is a plain number with no explanation in this file, so do not treat it as an official grading without checking how the app uses it.

sections.name: TaxonomyDocument
sections.title: Shape of one publication record
sections.what: Describes a single document a publisher has released, with a title, optional year, optional link and a format such as report, standard or handbook. Each document belongs to one publisher through its source id.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Records like this let a citation point to a specific document rather than to a publisher in general.
sections.watch_out: The source id must match a real publisher entry, otherwise the document cannot be traced back to its publisher.

sections.name: QuoteType
sections.title: Three levels of quote honesty
sections.what: Names the three ways a citation's text can relate to its source: exact quote, close paraphrase, or editorial summary. This tells a reader how literally the text can be trusted.
sections.why: The comments state the purpose: the label shows whether the text was checked word for word against the source.
sections.watch_out: Only the verbatim label means the text is exact, so anyone adding a citation must choose the label honestly.

sections.name: TaxonomyCitation
sections.title: Shape of one citation link
sections.what: Describes a single citation: which document it comes from, the excerpt text, how exact that text is, and optional section, link and note fields. Each citation ties a plant type to evidence for how it is classified.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the app show a user why a plant type was classified a certain way and how strong that evidence is.
sections.watch_out: Every citation in the data below is labelled paraphrased, so the app should not present any of them as exact quotes.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 1)
sections.title: Dairy and whey association publishers, part one
sections.what: Defines the first group of publishers: dairy and whey trade bodies such as the international dairy federation, the US dairy foods association and the European dairy association. Each has a short name, country, rank and description.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Entries are grouped with comments so they are easy to find.
sections.watch_out: The key of each record and its id field must match, because the code does not check that they agree.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 2)
sections.title: Dairy and whey association publishers, part two
sections.what: Continues the publisher list with the whey association and the European whey processors, then equipment makers such as Tetra Pak, GEA and SPX FLOW, and the start of the US government entries. The equipment makers are used as process references for dairy plants.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the group comments.
sections.watch_out: Equipment makers are typed as vendors, so their documents are supplier material rather than neutral standards, and the app should make that clear.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 3)
sections.title: Government and consulting publishers, part one
sections.what: Lists the US agriculture statistics and research bodies, the European statistics office, the international food standards body and the first group of consulting firms. These supply the official classifications and market data.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the group comments.
sections.watch_out: Consulting firm entries have no country, so the app cannot show a location for them.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 4)
sections.title: Consulting, trade and minerals publishers
sections.what: Finishes the consulting firm entries, then spreads in a shared brand list defined elsewhere, then adds trade magazines and the US geological survey and energy agency entries. These cover the mining and energy industries.
sections.why: Likely reason: the brand list is kept in a separate place so it can be reused. The code does not state this.
sections.watch_out: The shared brand list is referenced here but defined outside this file, so changes to it must be made in that other file.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_SOURCES (part 5)
sections.title: Energy and nuclear publishers, end of list
sections.what: Ends the publisher list with the energy agency description, the international atomic energy agency and the world nuclear association. These supply the reactor type references used for nuclear industries.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the descriptions.
sections.watch_out: The closing brackets must stay intact, because an error here stops the whole publisher list from loading.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_DOCUMENTS (part 1)
sections.title: Document records, first group
sections.what: Defines the first group of publication records, such as the Tetra Pak dairy handbook, the whey standards from the US dairy institute and the Codex dairy terms standard. Each has a title, year, link and format.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Documents are kept in one place so many citations can point to the same one.
sections.watch_out: Links and years are typed in by hand and can go out of date without any warning.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_DOCUMENTS (part 2)
sections.title: Document records, second group
sections.what: Continues the publication list with the US dairy economic report, the European dairy and whey reports, equipment brochures and the first consulting reports. Each is a document that citations can point to.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Some links go to general website pages rather than a fixed report, so the content behind them may change.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_DOCUMENTS (part 3)
sections.title: Document records, final group
sections.what: Finishes the publication list with the consulting construction survey, the critical minerals outlook, the US minerals summaries and the nuclear reactor database entries. The list ends here.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The publication list must stay in step with the publisher list, because a document pointing to a missing publisher is skipped when sources are collected.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 1)
sections.title: Citation evidence for dairy plants, first part
sections.what: Starts the citations, which are grouped first by industry and then by plant type name. For dairy it gives the evidence for fluid milk, cheese, butter and ghee plants, and begins the yogurt group, each with an excerpt and usually a section reference.
sections.why: The comments state the purpose: each citation includes an excerpt and a link so users can check the basis of a classification.
sections.watch_out: The plant type name must match the name in the industry tree exactly, or its citations will never be shown.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 2)
sections.title: Citation evidence for dairy plants, second part
sections.what: Continues the dairy citations for yogurt, milk powder and whey protein concentrate plants, each citing a standard or handbook excerpt. Some citations have no section reference.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the comment at the top of the citation list.
sections.watch_out: The excerpts are paraphrases written by whoever entered them, and this file cannot show that they match the sources word for word.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 3)
sections.title: Citation evidence for whey plants
sections.what: Gives citations for whey protein concentrate grades, whey protein isolate, whey hydrolysate, native whey and the start of demineralized whey. Each ties a plant type to a published grade or process description.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the group names.
sections.watch_out: The concentrate group is named 35 / 65 / 80 while one excerpt mentions a 34 grade, so check the grade numbers against the source.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 4)
sections.title: Citation evidence for casein, ice cream and formula
sections.what: Finishes the demineralized whey citations, then adds citations for casein, ice cream, infant formula and plant-based dairy plants. This closes the dairy section and begins the mining section.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The plant-based dairy citation has no section reference, which makes it harder to check than the others.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 5)
sections.title: Citation evidence for lithium and battery metals
sections.what: Gives citations for lithium deposit types and the battery metals group in the mining industry, sourced from the energy agency and the US geological survey. These feed the mining plant types.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The same citation text is reused for several plant types, so changing one excerpt changes all of them.

sections.name: TAXONOMY_CITATIONS (part 6)
sections.title: Citation evidence for nuclear reactors
sections.what: Gives the nuclear reactor construction citations, which name reactor type codes and small modular reactor categories from the atomic energy agency and the nuclear association. This closes the citation list.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: If a new reactor type is added to the nuclear tree, a matching citation must also be added or the new type will show nothing.

sections.name: getDocument
sections.title: Look up a publication by id
sections.what: Returns the publication record for the given id, or nothing if it is not in the list. This turns the id stored in a citation into the full document details.
sections.why: Likely reason: citations store only an id, so this lookup gives the full details when needed.
sections.watch_out: A missing id returns nothing rather than an error, so the caller must handle that case.

sections.name: getSource
sections.title: Look up a publisher by id
sections.what: Returns the publisher record for the given id, or nothing if none matches. This turns a publisher id into its full details.
sections.why: Likely reason: the same reason as the publication lookup, applied to publishers.
sections.watch_out: A missing id gives nothing with no warning, so a broken reference is easy to miss.

sections.name: getCitations
sections.title: Get citations for one plant type
sections.what: Returns the list of citations for a given industry and plant type name, or an empty list if there are none. Likely the source of the evidence shown when a user asks how a plant type was classified.
sections.why: Likely reason: returning an empty list instead of nothing means the caller never has to check for a missing value.
sections.watch_out: The plant type name is matched exactly, so a difference in spelling or spacing returns an empty list with no error.

sections.name: getIndustryTaxonomySources
sections.title: Collect all publishers for one industry
sections.what: Gathers every publisher behind any citation in an industry, without duplicates, and returns their records. This gives a list of sources for that industry without listing each citation.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the app show a summary of sources per industry.
sections.watch_out: Citations that point to a missing document or publisher are skipped silently, so a broken link makes a source disappear from the list.

summary: This file is the catalog of industries the app knows about, including each one's name, sector, status, and a tree of its sub-industries.
purpose: It gives the rest of the app one list of industries, each with the labels, the sub-industry tree, and the metrics the app should show for it. Other code looks industries up by slug, by sector, or to read their sources and citations.
why: Reason not stated in the code. The file is written as plain data so that industry content can be edited without changing program logic.
how: First it brings in brand constants and defines the allowed status and structure labels. Then it defines the shape of a tree node and an industry record. It lists the sectors, builds a shared note that names the consulting firms behind the taxonomy, and then lists each industry with its tree. The file ends with lookup functions and lists of taxonomy sources, documents and citations.
inputs: No runtime inputs. The data is written directly in the file, and the brand file supplies two extra lists of firm names.
outputs: Lists of industries and sectors, plus lookup helpers such as getting one industry by its slug or getting all industries in a sector. Callers also read the sub-industry trees, key metrics and taxonomy source lists.
risks: Renaming a node changes what counts as a valid subIndustry value, so existing records may stop matching. The dairy taxonomy note is cut off in the text provided, so its full wording cannot be checked here. Several industries are marked STUB, and the file does not say what that means for the user.
debug: If an industry is missing, search for its slug in this file and check the slug spelling used by the caller. If a subIndustry value is rejected, compare it with the node names under that industry's structure. If a sector lookup returns nothing, check that the industry's sector field matches a sector id in the sectors list.
